chunks: ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Ḥammād, from al-Ḥalabī, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, that he said:
Concerning a man who hired a worker and seated him over his belongings, then he stole from it, he said: “He is entrusted.”

And he said concerning a man who came to another man and said: “So-and-so sent me to you so that you may send to him such-and-such,” so he gave it to him and believed him. Then he met his companion and said to him: “Your messenger came to me, so I sent with him to you such-and-such.” He said: “I did not send him to you, and nothing came to me.” And the messenger claimed that he had indeed sent him and handed it over to him. So he said: “If he finds proof against him that he never sent him, his hand is cut off. But if he does not find proof, then his oath by Allah is: ‘I did not send him,’ and the other recovers the property from the messenger.”
I said: “What do you think if he claims that only need drove him to that?” He said: “He is to have his hand cut off, because he stole the man’s property.”

key_terms.الرَّسُولُ: the claimed messenger carrying or receiving property on another’s behalf
key_terms.الْحَاجَةُ: need or hardship claimed as the motive
key_terms.بَيِّنَةً: legal proof or evidentiary testimony establishing a claim
key_terms.سَرَقَ: he committed theft by unlawfully taking property
key_terms.قُطِعَتْ يَدُهُ: the legal hadd punishment of cutting off the hand for theft
key_terms.مُؤْتَمَنٌ: one regarded as entrusted with property
key_terms.يَمِينُهُ: his sworn oath used in adjudication when proof is absent

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on someone who fraudulently takes property by claiming to be another person’s messenger?
ai.summary: This hadith sets out legal rulings regarding theft, entrusted property, and fraudulent taking of another’s wealth by falsely claiming to be a messenger. It distinguishes between one who is treated as a trustee and one whose act is established as theft through proof or oath-based adjudication. It also states that need does not negate the ruling when the act is judged to be theft.
